title: “Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who do not know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, the escape as escape…
content: “Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who do not know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, the escape as escape in the case of forms — they will certainly not understand forms as they actually are, nor can they lead others to a similar position, namely, understanding forms as they actually are — such a thing is not possible. Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, the escape as escape in the case of forms — they will certainly understand forms as they actually are, and they can lead others to a similar position, namely, understanding forms as they actually are — such a thing is possible.”

title: “And what, monks, is the practice of restraint? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he does not grasp the general…
content: “And what, monks, is the practice of restraint? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — he restrains that cause, guards the eye faculty, practices restraint of the eye. When he hears a sound … smells an odor … tastes a flavor … feels a touch … cognizes a phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — he restrains that cause, guards the mind faculty, practices restraint of the mind. This, monks, is called the practice of restraint.”

title: “Poṭṭhapāda, I teach the Dhamma for the removal of gross personality view. If you practice accordingly, then defiling states are abandoned, pure states increase, and…
content: “Poṭṭhapāda, I teach the Dhamma for the removal of gross personality view. If you practice accordingly, then defiling states are abandoned, pure states increase, and in this very life, by direct knowledge, you realize and abide in full, vast wisdom. Poṭṭhapāda, you might think: ‘Defiling states will be abandoned, pure states will increase, and in this very life, by direct knowledge, one realizes and abides in full, vast wisdom — yet suffering still remains.’ Poṭṭhapāda, do not think thus. When defiling states are abandoned, pure states increase, and in this very life, by direct knowledge, one realizes and abides in full, vast wisdom — then gladness arises, joy, tranquility, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and a pleasant abiding arise.”

title: “Form is a lump of glowing ember, monks! Feeling is a lump of glowing ember! Perception is a lump of glowing ember! Formations are lumps…
content: “Form is a lump of glowing ember, monks! Feeling is a lump of glowing ember! Perception is a lump of glowing ember! Formations are lumps of glowing ember! Consciousness is a lump of glowing ember! Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, knowledge arises: ‘Liberated.’ He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

title: Standing to one side, a deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One: Among us humans, Sensual pleasures are impermanent. Whoever enjoys…
content:
Standing to one side, a deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
Among us humans,
Sensual pleasures are impermanent.
Whoever enjoys them here,
Is tied, bound by them.
Heedless regarding them,
Hard to escape from them —
One who cannot escape easily
Is conquered by Death.
Danger arises from sensual desire,
Suffering arises from sensual desire.
If sensual desire is subdued,
Then danger is subdued,
When danger is subdued,
Suffering is subdued.
The various objects in the world
Are not the sensual desires themselves —
It is the thought of greed
That is the sensual desire of humans.
The various objects remain
As they are in the world,
Therefore the wise
Subdue their sensual desires.
Abandon anger,
Subdue conceit,
Overcome all
Fetters that bind.
Do not cling excessively
To that name-and-form —
Suffering cannot reach
One who has nothing.
Give up calculations,
Do not chase after false thoughts,
Cut off all craving
For name-and-form in the world.
That one, free from defilements,
Without anxiety, without craving —
Gods and humans,
In this life or the next,
In heavenly realms
Or any dwelling place,
Seeking but not finding
The trace of that one —
They search but do not see
The one thus liberated.

title: “Suppose, monks, a fisherman throws a baited hook into a deep lake. A fish, seeing the bait, swallows the hook. Thus, monks, that fish, having…
content: “Suppose, monks, a fisherman throws a baited hook into a deep lake. A fish, seeing the bait, swallows the hook. Thus, monks, that fish, having swallowed the fisherman’s hook, has fallen into misfortune, into calamity, subject to the fisherman’s will. So too, monks, there are these six hooks in the world, leading to the misfortune of beings, to the calamity of living beings. What six? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in those forms, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — then that monk is called one who has swallowed Māra’s hook, has fallen into misfortune, into calamity, subject to the Evil One’s will. There are sounds … odors … tastes … touches … phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk delights in those phenomena, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — then that monk is called one who has swallowed Māra’s hook, has fallen into misfortune, into calamity, subject to the Evil One’s will.”

title: “Seeing the destruction of birth, The end of fetters, Destroying the path of sensual desire, Without remainder — That one is pure, faultless, Stainless, undefiled…
content:
“Seeing the destruction of birth,
The end of fetters,
Destroying the path of sensual desire,
Without remainder —
That one is pure, faultless,
Stainless, undefiled —
The Tathāgata is worthy of offerings.”

“One who does not see a self within the self,
Concentrated, upright, steady,
Without desire, without rigidity, without doubt —
The Tathāgata is worthy of offerings.”

“One in whom there is no root of delusion,
Who knows, who sees all things,
Who bears this last body —
Attaining perfect enlightenment,
The unsurpassed state of peace —
Thus is the Tathāgata, worthy of offerings.”

title: “‘Empty is the world, empty is the world,’ venerable sir, is said. To what extent, venerable sir, is it said that the world is empty?”…
content: “‘Empty is the world, empty is the world,’ venerable sir, is said. To what extent, venerable sir, is it said that the world is empty?” - “Ānanda, because the world is empty of self and anything belonging to self, therefore it is said that the world is empty. And what, Ānanda, is empty of self and anything belonging to self? The eye, Ānanda, is empty of self and anything belonging to self. Forms are empty of self and anything belonging to self. Eye-consciousness … Eye-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact … that feeling is empty of self and anything belonging to self. The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … The mind … Phenomena … Mind-consciousness … Mind-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact … that feeling is empty of self and anything belonging to self. And because it is empty of self and anything belonging to self, Ānanda, it is said that the world is empty.”

title: “And what, monks, is the practice of calming? Here, monks, a monk does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, calms, ends, and…
content: “And what, monks, is the practice of calming? Here, monks, a monk does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, calms, ends, and makes it non-existent. He does not consent to arisen ill-will thought … harmful thought … to arisen evil, unwholesome thoughts; he abandons, dispels, calms, ends, and makes them non-existent. This, monks, is called the practice of calming.”

title: “Monks, then I dwelt heedful, ardent, resolute. When a sensual thought arose, I understood: ‘This sensual thought has arisen in me, and it leads to…
content: “Monks, then I dwelt heedful, ardent, resolute. When a sensual thought arose, I understood: ‘This sensual thought has arisen in me, and it leads to my own harm, to others’ harm, to the harm of both, destroys wisdom, is part of vexation, does not lead to Nibbāna.’ Monks, as I reflected: ‘This sensual thought leads to my own harm’ – it subsided. As I reflected: ‘It leads to others’ harm’ – it subsided. As I reflected: ‘It leads to the harm of both’ – it subsided. As I reflected: ‘It destroys wisdom, is part of vexation, does not lead to Nibbāna’ – it subsided. Thus, monks, I continued to remove, abandon, and put an end to sensual thoughts.”
